entities.text: Mr.Arunkumar vs The Food Safety Officer
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The petitioner is the 1st accused in S.T.No.2677/2015 on the files of the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Kalamassery for having allegedly committed offences punishable under Sections 3(1) (zx), 3(1) (zz), (v) (x) Section 26(2) (i) (ii), Section 51,
Section 59 (i), 66 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act 'for short').

entities.text: Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Kalamassery
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The complaint was filed before the Judicial Magistrate on 17.11.2014.

The seizure of the food article was on 29.10.2013 and therefore the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner submits that there is delay of more than one year as stipulated under 77 of the FSS Act and therefore the complaint ought to have been rejected at the threshold.

He filed an application for discharge under Section 258 of Cr.P.C. and vide the impugned order at Annexure A8, the learned Magistrate found that in compliance of the proviso to Section 77 of the FSS Act, the Commissioner has vide Annexure A4 dated 18.10.2014 granted sanction for the prosecution to launch within a period of one month and within that period the prosecution has been launched.
It is also pertinent to note that the proviso to Section 77 specifically states that it is for the Commissioner of Food Safety to explain the reasons for the delay and grant further time.

There is reference made in Annexure A4 to the report of the Director of CFL, Kolkotta which is dated 30.06.2014 and it is on the basis of that the food article was found to be in contravention with the provisions of the Act.
The food article was sent for examination to the CFL at Kolkotta at the instance of the accused and without waiting for the report from there, no prosecution should have been launched.

2. The learned Additional Director General of Prosecution relies on the decision of State of Rajasthan v. Sanjay Kumar and others [1998 KHC 968] in support of his argument regarding the fact that under Section 469 Cr.P.C. also, the commencement of limitation of period can start only when the commission of offence was known to the person who is aggrieved by the offence or to the police officer.

entities.text: State of Rajasthan v. Sanjay Kumar and others [1998 KHC 968]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Under that provisions also the commission of offence could be said to have been revealed to the Food Safety Officer only on getting the report from the CFL, which is dated 30.06.2014 and within one year from that period, the complaint has been filed.

The Honourable Supreme Court has in the above cited decision held as follows:-
"13.

For the above reasons, in the instant case, the limitation for the purpose of S.468(2)(c) will commence from July 2, 1988, the date of knowledge of the commission of offence to the concerned officer under Section 469(1) (b) but not from February 29, 1988 (the date of collection of samples by the Drugs Inspector) and as the complaint was filed on June 28, 1991 which is within three years so the complaint is not barred by limitation under S.468(2) (c).

The High Court has missed this germane aspect and erroneously took the date of commencement of the limitation as February 29, 1988, the date on which the samples were collected by the Drugs Inspector from accused No.16.
It is thus clear that the High Court has committed illegality in so computing the period of limitation, which result in miscarriage of justice."

sentences.text: 2 In view of the decision of the Honourable Supreme Court and also the circumstances which led to the delay in filling the complaint and fully in agreement with the learned Magistrate in what he has observed in Annexure A8 order refusing to discharge the petitioner under Section 258 Cr.P.C., there is no reason to interfere with that order and hence the Crl.M.C is dismissed.
